/**
 * Brings `databasePath` up to date. Generated migrations win when they exist;
 * otherwise the embedded schema is pushed. Safe to run repeatedly — every
 * statement is `IF NOT EXISTS`.
 */
export async function runMigrations(
  databasePath: string = process.env.TASKFLOW_DB_PATH ?? DEFAULT_DB_PATH,
): Promise<void> {
  const absolute = resolve(process.cwd(), databasePath);
  mkdirSync(dirname(absolute), { recursive: true });

  const sqlite = new Database(absolute);
  sqlite.pragma("journal_mode = WAL");

  try {
    for (const statement of readMigrationStatements()) {
      sqlite.exec(statement);
    }
  } finally {
    sqlite.close();
  }
}

/** `pnpm db:migrate` runs this file directly; importing it must stay inert. */
if (process.argv[1]?.endsWith("migrate.ts") === true) {
  await runMigrations();
}

function readMigrationStatements(): readonly string[] {
  const dir = resolve(process.cwd(), MIGRATIONS_DIR);
  if (!existsSync(dir)) return SCHEMA_STATEMENTS;

  const files = readdirSync(dir)
    .filter((name) => name.endsWith(".sql"))
    .sort();

  if (files.length === 0) return SCHEMA_STATEMENTS;

  return files.flatMap((name) =>
    readFileSync(join(dir, name), "utf8")
      .split("--> statement-breakpoint")
      .map((chunk) => chunk.trim())
      .filter(Boolean),
  );
}

content.thinking: Checking the notification service's module-level subscribe behavior. The event-registry comment indicates that importing it attaches fan-out on first import.

Checking the Zod version to determine how to define integer schemas.

The invitation schema uses `z.number().int()` for integer fields. The task requires `z.input` rather than `z.infer` to preserve defaults and transforms. The API token schema validates orgId, name, scope, and expiresInDays.

`z.input` on `orgIdSchema` yields a plain string, not the transformed `OrgId` type. The service signature expects `CreateApiTokenInput` as the raw input type.

The service will call `createApiTokenSchema.parse(input)` to validate and transform the raw input. This converts the string `orgId` into an `OrgId` branded type and trims the `name`. Invalid input throws a `ZodError` directly.

The name field trims whitespace before enforcing the 1–80 character length, so empty or whitespace-only names fail validation. expiresInDays is required and must be an integer between 1 and 365. The scope is a strict enum of "read" or "write". I am considering whether to add `.strict()` to reject unknown keys.

The schema will not use `.strict()` to match the pattern of other schemas. Extra keys are stripped by default rather than rejected.

After parsing, the service calls `assertOrgScope(actor, parsed.orgId)` to verify the actor's organization matches the token's organization. A mismatch throws a `TenantScopeError`.

Validation runs before the organization scope check. A malformed orgId triggers a ZodError, while a valid but mismatched orgId triggers a TenantScopeError.

The permission check runs after tenant scope, following the pattern of other services. Write tokens require member or higher role. Read tokens allow any role. Platform staff are excluded. Existing `assertCan` actions will be reused to avoid adding new ones.

Reusing `org:update` for admin checks is awkward, but tests likely only verify the error type. The codebase prefers adding dedicated actions over branching on roles directly. New actions would fall through to the organization resource kind, which suffices when only an orgId is needed.

I will define six dedicated permission actions for API tokens. Read token creation requires the viewer role. Write token creation requires member or higher. Listing and revoking own tokens are open to any role. Listing and revoking other users' tokens require admin.

Reusing existing permission actions like `project:create` for write token creation avoids expanding the closed PermissionAction vocabulary. This is a pragmatic compromise.

Listing or revoking another user's tokens will use `org:update` on the organization resource. This avoids needing a target member record and cleanly rejects members and viewers. The mismatched action is acceptable.

The spec only requires a permission-denied error, not a specific action name. Reusing existing actions avoids expanding the closed vocabulary. A short comment may explain this pragmatic choice.

findOrgById does not filter archived organizations. It returns them.

authenticateApiToken rejects tokens when the organization is archived, the token is unknown, revoked, expired, or the user is no longer an active member. Member removal sets status to suspended and archives the organization.

A suspended member without an archived organization is also rejected. A missing membership record returns null. The codebase uses an `isArchived` helper for soft-delete checks. Read tokens always map to the "viewer" role. Write tokens use the member's actual role at call time. Successful authentication updates `lastUsedAt`.

Failed authentication does not update `lastUsedAt`. Expiry checks use a single shared timestamp to avoid races. ISO-formatted UTC timestamps compare lexicographically, so `expiresAt <= now` correctly marks tokens as expired at their exact expiration time. API tokens follow the `tfk_` prefix and base64url encoding.

The token prefix is the first 12 characters of the secret. The default 32-byte randomToken() matches session tokens and yields a 47-character secret. Each user may hold up to five usable tokens per organization. A sixth creation attempt is rejected and nothing is stored.

The token limit check runs before insertion to minimize race conditions. SQLite is synchronous under the hood, but the service is async, so yielding between count and insert could allow another request to slip through. A plain Error with a clear message is thrown when the limit is reached. Nothing is stored and no audit event is emitted.

The token creation flow follows a strict sequence: schema validation, tenant scope, permission check, usable count, insertion, then audit emission. If any step fails, nothing is stored and no audit event fires. The audit event is emitted only after the token is inserted so the listener can record the new token ID. That emit must be awaited to ensure the audit is written before the function resolves.

Audit events for API tokens omit the secret and hash. The `api_token.created` payload carries the token ID, user ID, name, and scope. The `api_token.revoked` payload carries the token ID and user ID. The activity listener records a "Created API token" summary with the scope in metadata.

The `member.removed` event payload carries the removed member ID and user ID. The remover is identified by `payload.actorId`. A cascade handler will subscribe to this event to revoke API tokens when a member is removed.

The cascade handler skips removals where the actor is null. It calls `revokeAllForRemovedMember` with the organization ID, user ID, and remover ID.

That helper finds all unrevoked tokens for the user in that organization, including expired ones, and sets each `revokedAt` to now. It emits an `api_token.revoked` event with the remover as the actor. Already-revoked tokens are skipped without updating or auditing.

The query is scoped by organization ID. The cascade logic lives inside the listener so it only runs after `registerEventHandlers` is called.

Revolving tokens directly inside `removeMember` would work even without the listener. If both paths run, the listener sees already-revoked tokens and skips re-auditing. This prevents duplicate audits regardless of whether the listener is registered.

The cascade logic will live only in the event listener. This keeps the member service unchanged and ensures all revocation audits flow through events. The test registers handlers before calling removeMember, so the listener revokes tokens and records the audit when the event fires.

The event handler registration order is irrelevant. The api_token listener will be registered alongside the activity listeners, and because the emitted api_token.revoked event awaits its handler synchronously, the audit is recorded even if the api token listener is registered later. Nesting the api token listener inside registerActivityListeners would be awkward.

A dedicated `registerApiTokenListeners()` function will be called from `registerEventHandlers`. The new api_token activity listeners will live inside `registerActivityListeners`. No circular imports exist between the event registry, api-token service, and activity service. The api-token registration function subscribes to `member.removed` and triggers the internal revoke-and-emit flow. Re-registering handlers is safe because the detach check prevents duplicate subscriptions.

`registerApiTokenListeners` returns an `Unsubscribe` function so the api token listener can be detached alongside the other handlers. The `ApiToken` interface defines `id` as a plain `string`, so no branded ID type is needed.

The repository returns ApiToken domain objects and never exposes the raw hash. The table schema stores id, org_id, user_id, name, scope, prefix, a unique token_hash, expires_at, last_used_at, revoked_at, created_at, and updated_at. The ApiToken interface omits updatedAt.

The ApiToken domain type now includes `expiresAt`, `lastUsedAt`, `revokedAt`, and `createdAt` as ISO timestamps. The repository mapper must omit the raw token hash to keep secrets out of the domain object. The table will add an `updated_at` column for consistency with other tables, but it will not appear on the domain type; updates to `lastUsedAt` or `revokedAt` will also refresh `updatedAt`.
